en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Chapter on Similes, Section on the Jar.
7. The Question on the Factors of Archery “Venerable Nāgasena, as for what you say—that ‘four factors of an archer are to be adopted’—which are those four factors to be adopted?
“Just as, Great King, an archer, when discharging an arrow, firmly plants both feet upon the ground;”
He makes his knees uneven; he places a bundle of grass at the junction of his waist; he makes his body rigid;
he fixes his two hands upon the joints; he clenches his fists; he makes his fingers touch one another without gaps;
he stiffens his neck; he closes his eyes and mouth; he straightens the sign; and he arouses laughter, thinking, "I shall pierce it."
In the same way, great king, a yogi, a practitioner of yoga, should establish himself on the earth of virtue with the feet of energy;
he should make patience and gentleness his support; he should fix his mind on restraint; he should apply himself to self-control and discipline;
he should suppress desire and infatuation; and he should make his mind continuous in wise attention.
“Energy must be exerted, the six doors must be closed, mindfulness must be established, and joy must be generated with the thought:
‘I shall pierce all defilements with the arrow of knowledge.
This, Great King, is the first quality of an archer that must be acquired.”
Furthermore, Great King, an archer carries a whetting-stone to straighten an arrow that is crooked, bent, or curved.
In the same way, Great King, a practitioner of yoga must carry the whetting-stone of mindfulness established upon this body to straighten a mind that is crooked, bent, or curved.
This, Great King, is the second quality to be adopted from the archer.
Furthermore, Great King, an archer practices at the target;
even so, Great King, must this body be practiced upon by the yogin, the practitioner of yoga.
How, Great King, must this body be practiced upon by the yogin, the practitioner of yoga?
It should be attended to as impermanent, it should be attended to as suffering, it should be attended to as non-self; as a disease...
as a tumor...
as a dart...
As suffering... as an affliction...
as the other...
As disintegration,
as calamity,
as misfortune...
As fear...
as an affliction...
as instability...
...from its perishable nature ...
from its unstable nature ...
from its lack of refuge ...
...as being without shelter...
as being without refuge...
as being empty...
As empty … as void … as a danger …
As subject to change,
as lacking essence,
and as the root of suffering...
As a murderer...
as non-existence...
as subject to taints...
From the perspective of being conditioned... from the perspective of being the bait of Māra...
from the perspective of being subject to birth...
From the nature of aging … from the nature of illness … from the nature of death …
from the nature of sorrow … from the nature of lamentation … from the nature of despair …
"By way of its nature as subject to defilement...
Thus, Great King, should this body be contemplated by a yogi, a practitioner of yoga.
This, Great King, is the third quality of the archer that should be adopted."
Furthermore, great king, an archer practices his aim morning and evening;
even so, great king, a yogi who is a practitioner of yoga should practice his object of focus morning and evening.
This, great king, is the fourth quality to be adopted from the archer.
This was said, Great King, by the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma:
“Just as an archer, for instance,
practices evening and morning;”
Not neglecting his service,
he receives food and wages;
even so does the son of the Buddha.
“He practices the cultivation of the body;
by not neglecting the cultivation of the body,
he attains arahantship.”
The seventh question on the archer.
The seventh chapter, the Chapter on the Jar.
Its summary verse:
Kumbha and Kāḷāyasa,
the parasol, the field, and the antidote;
and with food, Issāsa.
"Now it has been stated by the wise.
The Question on Similes is finished.
